t: LeetCode 1686 — Stone Game VI: Both Players Race for the Same a+b Order
o:
Alice and Bob alternately remove stones; the taker banks his own valuation. Reframe the game around the final difference D = Alice - Bob: Alice taking stone i raises D by a_i, Bob taking it lowers D by b_i, so relative to conceding the stone to the opponent, stone i is worth a_i + b_i to whoever grabs it - and that combined value is identical for both players.

Example 1: sums are 3 (stone 0) and 4 (stone 1), so Alice grabs stone 1 for +3, Bob settles for stone 0 at -2, and Alice wins. Example 2 ends with both on 1 point (draw). Example 3 shows Bob outscores Alice no matter what she does.

With n up to 10^5, exponential minimax is only a conceptual baseline; the real solution sorts once by a_i + b_i and simulates.
k: Stone i has strategic worth aliceValues[i] + bobValues[i] to either player - the swing it causes in the score difference.
Taking the current maximum-sum stone is always safe: an exchange argument shows swapping any other choice with it never hurts the mover.
Ties in combined value do not affect the outcome - equal-sum stones contribute the same net swing however their order is permuted.

a.i: Model the game directly: f(mask) is the current player’s best achievable own-score-minus-opponent-score given the set of removed stones in mask; whose turn it is follows from the popcount. Correct and instructive, but the state space is exponential, so this only serves tiny inputs.
s: f(mask) returns 0 when all stones are gone.
Otherwise try every remaining stone i; the gain is aliceValues[i] on Alice turns (even popcount), else bobValues[i].
Recurse as gain - f(mask | 1 << i): the formula flips perspective each turn, so negation carries the opponent’s best reply.
Take the maximum over all moves and memoize per mask.
The sign of f(0) decides the printed answer.
a.t: O(2^n * n) — every reachable stone subset is expanded once with n candidate moves

a.i: Sort stones by aliceValues + bobValues descending and simulate: Alice (even turns) adds her valuation, Bob subtracts his. Why optimal: whenever a player skips the highest-sum remaining stone s in favor of another t, exchanging the two picks leaves all earlier decisions unchanged and changes the mover’s margin by sum(s) - sum(t) >= 0 regardless of who eventually takes each stone - so grabbing s first is dominant, and induction finishes the proof.
s: Pair each index with a_i + b_i and sort the indices descending by that sum.
Walk the sorted order, alternating turns starting with Alice.
Add a_i for Alice picks; subtract b_i for Bob picks.
Report 1 / -1 / 0 according to the sign of the running difference.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; the sweep is linear

w:
Derive the swing identity in the interview - it collapses the entire game into one sort. Then note why ties are harmless and why the exchange argument needs no case analysis on who takes which stone.
Pitfall: greedily maximizing only your own values loses positions where denial matters - e.g. aliceValues = [2, 5], bobValues = [9, 0]: grabbing your personal max (5) hands Bob the 9 and loses, while the a+b rule takes the 9-valued stone first and wins.
The minimax draft also breaks past n ~ 30 because bitmask shifts exceed 32 bits in some languages. Follow-ups: more than two players, per-turn score multipliers, or reconstructing the optimal pick sequence.
